summary: Defines the initial entries for the IANA Registry of Performance Metrics, including UDP round-trip latency and loss, packet delay variation, DNS response latency and loss, ICMP round-trip latency and loss, and TCP round-trip delay and loss. It is standards-track.

eli5.summary: This document fills the first pages of a catalog of network measurements, like how long messages take and how many get lost, for several kinds of traffic.

subtitle: The baseline catalog of standardized network performance measurements.

tldr.problem: Network performance varies widely, and different measurement methods produce incomparable results. No standard registry existed for publishing performance metrics in a way that allowed operators and researchers to coordinate on what to measure and how.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8912 defines the initial set of entries in the IANA Performance Metrics Registry, specifying standardized methods and definitions for measuring delay, loss, and jitter in UDP, DNS, ICMP, and TCP traffic over IP networks.
tldr.outcome: Networks can now use a common language for performance metrics, with precise definitions of measurement parameters, data formats, and output statistics, enabling consistent monitoring and benchmarking across different systems.

facts.label: Loss threshold (Tmax)
facts.value: 3.0 seconds for UDP and ICMP, 5.0 for DNS

today: RFC 8912 published in November 2021 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. The Performance Metrics Registry at IANA contains these initial entries and is open to new entries submitted through the IETF standards process.

sections.title: The Performance Metrics Registry
sections.content:
Networks need to measure how well they are performing: how fast is a message delivered, how many packets are lost, how much does latency vary. But different teams measure these things in different ways, making results hard to compare. RFC 8912 establishes the IANA Performance Metrics Registry, a formal catalog of standardized metrics with precise definitions of how to measure them.

The registry builds on decades of IPPM (IP Performance Metrics) work from the IETF. Each metric in the registry specifies the type of traffic, packet parameters (size, headers, protocol), the measurement method, the equipment roles, the timeout threshold for declaring a packet lost, and the statistical output (mean, percentile, min, max).
sections.eli5: Different people measure the internet in different ways, making their results hard to compare. This is a rulebook saying 'if we all measure this way, our numbers will match'.

sections.title: Registry Structure and Parameters
sections.content:
Each metric entry in the registry includes five categories of information. The Summary category assigns a unique numeric ID, a human-readable name, and a URI. The Metric Definition specifies the reference RFC(s) and the fixed parameters: the exact packet structure, headers, protocols, and timeouts used in measurement.

The Method of Measurement category details how to generate the test traffic, how the measurement process should work, the roles of source and destination hosts, and runtime parameters (like measurement start and end times, source and destination addresses). The Output category defines what statistics are calculated and their format. Finally, the Administrative section records status, version, and the requester information.
sections.eli5: Each metric is like a recipe: ingredients (fixed parameters), steps (method), and what you measure at the end (output). Every recipe has a number and a name so everyone can find it.

sections.title: UDP and Passive Probing Metrics
sections.content:
The initial registry includes metrics for UDP round-trip latency and loss, measured by sending periodic UDP packets between two hosts and recording the delay and whether each packet arrived within a timeout window (Tmax = 3 seconds). The output is the 95th percentile of delay (for packets that arrived) and the loss ratio (lost packets divided by total packets sent).

The registry also defines packet delay variation (PDV): the difference in delay between successive packets. Jitter is important for real-time applications like voice and video. A separate set of entries covers DNS response latency and loss, measuring how long DNS queries take to be answered. These use Poisson-distributed (random-spacing) UDP packets to avoid synchronization effects.

One-way delay metrics measure individual packet trips rather than round-trips, using periodic UDP streams with fixed inter-packet spacing (20 milliseconds). The output includes statistics like the 95th percentile, mean, minimum, maximum, and standard deviation of delay.
sections.eli5: You send numbered packets out and measure how long they take to come back. If none come back in 3 seconds, you mark it lost. You record the time for each packet and calculate percentiles and averages.

sections.title: ICMP and TCP Round-Trip Metrics
sections.content:
The registry includes ICMP round-trip latency and loss metrics, which use ICMP Echo Request (ping) packets. ICMP probes are useful because many hosts respond to them and firewalls often allow them. The metric uses a SendOnRcv strategy: if a reply arrives quickly, send the next probe after a fixed interval; if the reply is slow or lost, adapt the interval accordingly. This avoids overwhelming slow hosts.

TCP round-trip delay and loss metrics measure the delay to establish a TCP connection (the time from sending a SYN to receiving a SYN-ACK) and whether the connection succeeds. These metrics are useful for measuring application-layer performance, since TCP is what most services use. The fixed parameters specify the target port (default 443 for HTTPS), packet size, and timeout threshold.

All metrics specify Tmax, the maximum waiting time before declaring a packet or response lost. This threshold is crucial: packets delayed beyond Tmax are excluded from delay statistics but counted as losses. Different metrics use different Tmax values depending on the protocol and use case.
sections.eli5: We also measure ping (ICMP echo) and website connections (TCP). Ping is quick and simple; TCP connection is more realistic for real web traffic.

sections.title: Precision and Calibration
sections.content:
Each metric specifies the exact packet structure: IPv4 and IPv6 headers, DSCP markings (usually 0 for best-effort), TTL (255 for local networks), protocol numbers (17 for UDP, 1 for ICMP, 6 for TCP), and payload sizes. For example, UDP round-trip metrics use 100-byte payloads, while DNS uses a complete DNS query message.

The measurement method distinguishes between truly lost packets and merely delayed ones. A packet is lost if it does not arrive within Tmax seconds. The RFC specifies that delay calculations use only successfully arrived packets, excluding lost ones from the delay statistics. For statistics like percentiles, the definition of percentile follows RFC 2330: the smallest delay value where the empirical distribution function reaches the target percentile (e.g., 95%).

Calibration is important for accuracy. The RFC recommends an internal loopback test at the source host to measure systematic and random errors. Clock synchronization between source and destination is critical for one-way metrics; the RFC requires reporting time offsets from a reference clock (NTP) to document synchronization accuracy.
sections.eli5: The rules say exactly what packets look like, how long to wait before giving up, and how to do the math. There are even instructions for checking if your measurement device is accurate.

sections.title: The Initial Registry Entries
sections.content:
RFC 8912 registers 27 initial metric entries, numbered 1 through 27. Entries 1-2 are UDP round-trip delay and loss. Entries 3 is packet delay variation (95th percentile). Entries 4-5 are DNS response latency and loss. Entries 6-11 measure UDP one-way delay (5 statistical variants: 95th percentile, mean, min, max, standard deviation) and one-way loss. Entries 12-17 are periodic UDP one-way metrics (using a fixed 20-millisecond interval). Entries 18-21 are ICMP round-trip metrics (mean, min, max, and loss). Entries 22-27 are TCP metrics measuring connection establishment delay.

Each metric entry includes a fully qualified name that documents the traffic type, measurement method, packet payload size, and output statistic. For example, RTDelay_Active_IP-UDP-Periodic_RFC8912sec4_Seconds_95Percentile means: round-trip delay of active UDP probes with periodic spacing, as defined in RFC 8912 section 4, output in seconds as a 95th percentile value. This naming convention allows the registry to expand while keeping names unambiguous.
sections.eli5: The RFC creates 27 recipes in the catalog. Each one has a unique number and a detailed name that describes exactly what it measures and how.

sections.title: IANA Registry and Future Extension
sections.content:
The Performance Metrics Registry is managed by IANA under the Specification Required policy, meaning new entries must be reviewed and approved by the IETF community before registration. This ensures quality and consistency. Each entry must cite an RFC or standards document that defines the metric, and provide all the registry columns with complete, precise definitions.

The registry is backward-compatible and extensible. Future RFCs can register new metrics following the same template and structure, using the next available numeric IDs. The naming convention ensures that new metrics can coexist with existing ones. This allows the registry to accommodate new protocols, new measurement strategies, and new output statistics without breaking existing entries.
sections.eli5: IANA keeps the official list and makes sure only good, well-documented recipes get added. New recipes can be added later, always with a new number, so the old ones keep working.
